word: wear one's heart on one's sleeve

senses: To show your feelings openly, so that everyone can see how you feel.

etymology: Shakespeare's Iago says "I will wear my heart upon my sleeve" in Othello (1604); the exact earlier origin is uncertain.

conversation.text: Jake wears his heart on his sleeve. If he's upset, you'll know it in two seconds.
I've always worn my heart on my sleeve, so poker is not my game.

core.definition: To let your emotions show plainly instead of hiding them, especially love, hurt or excitement.

pronunciation.respelling: wair wuhnz hahrt ahn wuhnz SLEEV
pronunciation.tip: Stress SLEEVE most, with a lighter beat on HEART. Both "one's" shrink to a quick wuhnz; in real speech they become "my," "her," "his."

nuance.connotation: Neutral to affectionate; it can suggest honesty and warmth, or that someone is easily hurt.
nuance.usage_note: Used to describe a person's character: "She wears her heart on her sleeve." The possessive matches the subject both times (my...my, his...his). It often carries a hint that the person could get hurt because they don't protect themselves.
word_family: wore one's heart on one's sleeve (past)

distinctions.note: An "open book" is a person whose thoughts and life are easy to know; "wear one's heart on one's sleeve" is specifically about showing feelings.
"Speak one's mind" is saying your opinions directly; "wear one's heart on one's sleeve" is letting your emotions show, with or without words.

antonyms: play one's cards close to the chest
collocations: wears her heart on her sleeve
has always worn his heart on his sleeve
someone who wears their heart on their sleeve
not one to wear his heart on his sleeve

examples.everyday: My dad wears his heart on his sleeve; he cried at my graduation and didn't care who saw.
examples.professional: He wears his heart on his sleeve in meetings, which makes him easy to read in negotiations.
examples.analytical: People who wear their hearts on their sleeves are often perceived as more trustworthy, though they may also be seen as less composed.

nuance.analogy: Like pinning your feelings to the outside of your clothes where anyone can read them.
nuance.etymology: Shakespeare's Iago says "I will wear my heart upon my sleeve" in Othello (1604); the exact earlier origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Saying "wear one's heart in one's sleeve"; it is "on".
Mixing possessives: "He wears my heart on his sleeve" means something else; use the same person twice.

word: at the end of one's rope

senses: Having no patience, strength or ideas left; unable to cope any longer.

etymology: Origin uncertain; the image is of reaching the end of a rope or tether, with nothing more to hold or let out. "At the end of one's tether" is the British form.

conversation.text: The baby hasn't slept in three nights. I'm at the end of my rope.
After the fourth call to customer service, I was at the end of my rope.

core.definition: So tired, frustrated or worried that you feel you can't take any more.

pronunciation.respelling: at thee end uhv wuhnz ROHP
pronunciation.tip: Stress ROPE. "The" before "end" is usually thee. American speakers say "rope"; British speakers prefer "tether."

nuance.connotation: Negative: it expresses exhaustion and desperation, often asking for sympathy or help.
nuance.usage_note: Usually with "be": "I'm at the end of my rope." It suits ongoing stress (a sick child, a bad boss, endless problems), not one small annoyance. It is the standard American form; "at the end of my tether" sounds British.

distinctions.note: "At one's wits' end" stresses not knowing what to do next; "at the end of one's rope" stresses having no patience or strength left. They often overlap.
"Fed up" is annoyed and tired of something; "at the end of one's rope" is closer to desperate.

collocations: I'm at the end of my rope
was at the end of her rope
at the end of their rope with
almost at the end of my rope

examples.everyday: With the kitchen torn up for two months, we're at the end of our rope.
examples.professional: Several nurses told management they were at the end of their rope after months of double shifts.
examples.analytical: Caregivers at the end of their rope are at higher risk of burnout, which is why respite programs matter.

nuance.analogy: Like climbing down a rope and finding there's nothing left to hold on to.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; the image is of reaching the end of a rope or tether, with nothing more to hold or let out. "At the end of one's tether" is the British form.
common_mistakes: Saying "at the end of my ropes"; it is singular.
Using "the end of the line" for this; that means the final stop or the end of something, not running out of patience.

senses: To annoy or upset someone, especially in a way that stays with them.
To affect someone strongly and stay in their thoughts (of a song, a person, an idea).

etymology: The image is of something working its way beneath the skin, like a splinter or an itch; the positive sense was popularized by the Cole Porter song "I've Got You Under My Skin" (1936).

conversation.text: Don't let his comments get under your skin. He says that to everyone.
That song really got under my skin. I've been humming it all week.

core.definition: To bother someone deeply, or to stay in their mind and feelings for a long time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SKIN. "Get under" links: geh-TUHN-der in quick speech.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative (irritation); can be positive when something moves or fascinates you.
nuance.usage_note: Very common as advice: "Don't let it get under your skin." Also "He really gets under my skin" for a person who always irritates you. The positive sense is common with music, books and people you are falling for.

distinctions.note: "Get on someone's nerves" is surface irritation from repeated small things; "get under someone's skin" goes deeper and lasts longer.
"Push someone's buttons" means deliberately provoking someone; "get under someone's skin" does not have to be deliberate.

collocations: don't let it get under your skin
knows how to get under his skin

examples.everyday: The way he chews gum really gets under my skin.
examples.professional: Try not to let one harsh review get under your skin; most customers are happy.
examples.analytical: Criticism that gets under a person's skin often touches an existing insecurity rather than the facts at hand.

nuance.analogy: Like a splinter: small, but once it's under the skin you can't stop feeling it.
nuance.etymology: The image is of something working its way beneath the skin, like a splinter or an itch; the positive sense was popularized by the Cole Porter song "I've Got You Under My Skin" (1936).
common_mistakes: Saying "get on someone's skin"; the preposition is "under".
Forgetting the person: say "It gets under my skin," not "It gets under skin."

senses: To annoy or irritate someone very much.

etymology: Origin uncertain; the image is of someone so agitated they want to climb the walls. Recorded from the mid-1900s.

conversation.text: The neighbor's dog barks all night. It's driving me up the wall.
My brother leaves the cabinets open, and it drives my mom up the wall.

core.definition: To make someone extremely annoyed, frustrated or close to losing their patience.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WALL. Many Americans say wall with the same vowel as "doll" (wahl); both are fine.

nuance.connotation: Negative, but usually used for everyday annoyances, often humorously.
nuance.usage_note: Usually in the progressive or present: "It's driving me up the wall," "He drives me up the wall." The subject is the annoying thing or person. Close to "drive someone crazy" and "drive someone nuts."

distinctions.note: "Drive someone crazy" is the most common everyday version; "up the wall" is slightly more vivid and informal.
"Climb the walls" means feeling restless or trapped (bored, anxious); "drive someone up the wall" means annoying them.

collocations: it's driving me up the wall
is going to drive me up the wall

examples.everyday: This slow Wi-Fi is driving me up the wall.
examples.professional: The constant changes to the schedule are driving the crew up the wall.
examples.analytical: Small recurring frustrations, the kind that drive people up the wall, can predict job dissatisfaction better than single big problems.

nuance.analogy: Like being so irritated you'd rather climb the walls than stay in the room.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; the image is of someone so agitated they want to climb the walls. Recorded from the mid-1900s.
common_mistakes: Saying "drive someone on the wall"; it is "up the wall".
Leaving out the object: say "It drives me up the wall," not "It drives up the wall."

senses: To talk to someone for a very long time, more than they want.

etymology: American, 20th century; a humorous exaggeration.

conversation.text: The guy next to me on the plane talked my ear off for three hours.
Sorry, I've been talking your ear off. How are you doing?

core.definition: To keep talking to someone on and on, so they can barely get away or speak.

pronunciation.tip: Stress EAR. "Ear off" links: ee-RAWF.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative or humorous; often used about yourself as a friendly apology.
nuance.usage_note: Common in "talked my ear off" and the self-aware "Sorry, I'm talking your ear off." It is gentle, not insulting; you can say it about a chatty grandparent with affection.

distinctions.note: "Bend someone's ear" is to talk to someone at length, often about a problem or to persuade them; "talk someone's ear off" is just talking far too much.
When someone talks your ear off, you can't "get a word in edgewise."

collocations: sorry for talking your ear off
will talk your ear off about
talked his ear off the whole way

examples.everyday: My aunt will talk your ear off about her garden if you let her.
examples.professional: The vendor talked my ear off at the conference, but the product actually looks useful.
examples.analytical: Researchers note that people tend to underestimate how much listeners enjoy a conversation, even when they fear they're talking someone's ear off.

nuance.analogy: Like talking so much that the listener's ear could fall off from use.
nuance.etymology: American, 20th century; a humorous exaggeration.
common_mistakes: Saying "talk someone's ears off"; the idiom uses the singular "ear".
Leaving out "off": "talk my ear" is not idiomatic.

senses: To deliberately say or do things that you know will annoy or upset someone.

etymology: From the image of pressing buttons on a machine to make it do something; American, late 20th century.

conversation.text: My little sister knows exactly how to push my buttons.
Don't react. He's just trying to push your buttons.

core.definition: To provoke someone on purpose by touching their sensitive spots.

pronunciation.tip: Stress BUTTONS on its first syllable: BUHT-nz. Americans say the middle t as a quick stop in the throat.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it implies teasing or provoking, sometimes playful, often mean.
nuance.usage_note: Often with "know how to": "She knows how to push my buttons." Also "He's pushing my buttons today." It suggests the person understands you well enough to target your weak points.

distinctions.note: "Get under someone's skin" can happen by accident; "push someone's buttons" is usually on purpose.
"Strike a nerve" is touching a sensitive subject, often unintentionally; "push someone's buttons" is repeated, deliberate provoking.

collocations: knows how to push my buttons

examples.everyday: Teenagers are experts at pushing their parents' buttons.
examples.professional: One board member seems to enjoy pushing the CFO's buttons during reviews.
examples.analytical: Provocation works by pushing a person's buttons: it predicts the emotional reaction and uses it to gain control.

nuance.analogy: Like a machine with buttons: press the right one and you get the same reaction every time.
nuance.etymology: From the image of pressing buttons on a machine to make it do something; American, late 20th century.
common_mistakes: Saying "press someone's buttons" is fine, but "push someone's button" (singular) is less common for this sense.
"Push all the right buttons" is positive: it means appealing perfectly to someone.

senses: To offend someone by getting involved in something that is their responsibility or territory.

etymology: The image is of physically treading on someone's foot, as when dancing too close.

conversation.text: I don't want to step on anyone's toes, but I have an idea for the marketing plan.
My mother-in-law kept rearranging my kitchen. She really stepped on my toes.

core.definition: To upset someone by doing their job, making their decisions or entering their area without being asked.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TOES. "Step on" links: steh-PAHN.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it means overstepping, though people often use it to show they want to avoid that.
nuance.usage_note: Very common as a polite disclaimer: "I don't want to step on anyone's toes, but..." Also "Am I stepping on your toes?" Works at work and at home; the plural "toes" is fixed.

distinctions.note: "Overstep (one's authority/bounds)" is the formal word; "step on someone's toes" is the friendly idiom.
"Ruffle someone's feathers" means upsetting someone in general; "step on someone's toes" is specifically intruding on their role.

collocations: don't want to step on anyone's toes
worried about stepping on her toes

examples.everyday: I'll let my sister plan the party; I don't want to step on her toes.
examples.professional: Before you contact the client directly, check with the account manager so you don't step on any toes.
examples.analytical: In organizations with unclear roles, people avoid initiative because they fear stepping on others' toes.

nuance.analogy: Like dancing too close: you end up on someone else's feet.
nuance.etymology: The image is of physically treading on someone's foot, as when dancing too close.
common_mistakes: Saying "step on someone's foot"; the idiom uses "toes".
Using it for physical pain only; in conversation it almost always means overstepping.

word: give someone a piece of one's mind
phonetic: /ˌɡɪv ˌsʌmwʌn ə ˌpis əv wʌnz ˈmaɪnd/

senses: To tell someone angrily and directly what you think of their behavior.

etymology: From the older sense of mind as opinion or intention; the phrase is several centuries old.

conversation.text: If the landlord doesn't fix the heat, I'm going to give him a piece of my mind.
She gave the driver who cut her off a piece of her mind.

core.definition: To scold someone frankly and angrily because they did something you think is wrong.

pronunciation.ipa: /ˌɡɪv ˌsʌmwʌn ə ˌpis əv wʌnz ˈmaɪnd/
pronunciation.respelling: giv suhm-wuhn uh pees uhv wuhnz MAHYND
pronunciation.tip: Stress MIND. "Piece of" links: PEE-suhv.

nuance.connotation: Negative and forceful; usually justified anger in the speaker's view.
nuance.usage_note: Often as a threat or plan: "I'm going to give him a piece of my mind." The two possessives differ: "give HIM a piece of MY mind." It suggests one heated conversation, not a long feud.
word_family: gave someone a piece of one's mind (past)

distinctions.note: "Tell someone off" means the same and is a bit more casual; "give someone a piece of one's mind" sounds more indignant.
"Read someone the riot act" is a stern warning, often by someone with authority; "a piece of one's mind" is personal anger, from anyone.

collocations: give him a piece of my mind
gave her a piece of his mind
going to give them a piece of my mind
wanted to give him a piece of my mind

examples.everyday: When the repair guy didn't show up again, I called and gave him a piece of my mind.
examples.professional: It is tempting to give a rude customer a piece of your mind, but escalate to a manager instead.
examples.analytical: Venting, or giving someone a piece of your mind, rarely calms anger as much as people expect.

nuance.analogy: Like handing someone a chunk of your angry thoughts to take home.
nuance.etymology: From the older sense of mind as opinion or intention; the phrase is several centuries old.
common_mistakes: Saying "give someone a part of my mind"; it is "piece".
Using it for friendly advice; it means scolding.

senses: To answer someone angrily and sharply, usually when they did not deserve it.

etymology: An exaggerated image of an angry animal snapping at someone.

conversation.text: Sorry I bit your head off this morning. I was stressed about the meeting.
I only asked if she was ready, and she bit my head off.

core.definition: To snap at someone with an angry reply out of proportion to what they said.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HEAD. "Head off" links: heh-DAWF.

nuance.connotation: Negative; often used in apologies or complaints about someone's overreaction.
nuance.usage_note: Very common in apologies: "Sorry, I didn't mean to bite your head off." Also as a request: "Don't bite my head off, I'm just asking." It describes a sudden short outburst, not a long argument.

distinctions.note: "Jump down someone's throat" means almost the same; it can suggest a bit more attacking or criticizing.
"Snap at someone" is the plain phrasal verb; "bite someone's head off" is more vivid.

collocations: sorry I bit your head off

examples.everyday: Don't bite my head off; I just asked where the remote is.
examples.professional: When the deadline slipped, the director bit the analyst's head off, and later apologized.
examples.analytical: Under stress, people are more likely to bite someone's head off, because irritability rises when sleep and patience run low.

nuance.analogy: Like a guard dog snapping at anyone who comes near.
nuance.etymology: An exaggerated image of an angry animal snapping at someone.
common_mistakes: Saying "bite someone's head"; you need "off".
Taking it literally or as very serious; it describes a sharp reply, not violence.

senses: To criticize or react angrily to someone suddenly, before they have finished or without good reason.

etymology: Origin uncertain; the image is of attacking the place where someone's words come from.

conversation.text: I barely started explaining, and he jumped down my throat.
Hey, don't jump down my throat. I'm just asking a question.

core.definition: To attack someone verbally the moment they say something, often unfairly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress THROAT. The "thr" needs your tongue between your teeth, then a quick r.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it complains about an unfair, too-fast reaction.
nuance.usage_note: Often as "Don't jump down my throat" or "Why did you jump down my throat?" It suggests the listener reacted before hearing the whole story.

distinctions.note: "Bite someone's head off" is a sharp, short angry reply; "jump down someone's throat" suggests attacking or accusing.
"Fly off the handle" is losing your temper in general; "jump down someone's throat" is aimed at a person.

antonyms: give someone the benefit of the doubt
collocations: no need to jump down my throat

examples.everyday: I asked if dinner was ready and she jumped down my throat.
examples.professional: If we jump down people's throats when they report mistakes, they'll stop reporting them.
examples.analytical: In heated online threads, users often jump down each other's throats before reading the whole post.

nuance.analogy: Like leaping on someone's words before they're even out of their mouth.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; the image is of attacking the place where someone's words come from.
common_mistakes: Saying "jump on someone's throat"; it is "down".
"Jump on someone" is close and also common, but don't mix them into "jump on someone's throat".

senses: Arguing or fighting angrily with each other, often again and again.

etymology: From the image of animals or fighters grabbing each other by the throat.

conversation.text: The kids have been at each other's throats all day.
The two parties are at each other's throats over the budget.

core.definition: In a state of bitter, continuing conflict with one another.

pronunciation.tip: Stress THROATS. "Each other's" links: ee-CHUH-therz.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it describes hostile, heated conflict.
nuance.usage_note: Usually with "be": "They're always at each other's throats." It describes two people or groups, never one. Common in news about rivals, politicians or teams.

distinctions.note: "At odds" means disagreeing; "at each other's throats" means fighting angrily.
"Bad blood" is long-standing hatred or resentment; "at each other's throats" describes the open fighting.

antonyms: get along like a house on fire
collocations: have been at each other's throats

examples.everyday: My roommates were at each other's throats over the dishes.
examples.professional: The two departments were at each other's throats until the reorganization clarified who owned what.
examples.analytical: When resources shrink, coalition partners often end up at each other's throats.

nuance.analogy: Like two dogs locked in a fight that neither will end.
nuance.etymology: From the image of animals or fighters grabbing each other by the throat.
common_mistakes: Saying "at each others' throats" or "at each others throats"; the possessive is "each other's".
Using it about one person: you need two sides.

senses: A person who loves socializing and moves easily from one group or conversation to another.

etymology: From the image of a butterfly flitting from flower to flower.

conversation.text: Maria is a total social butterfly. She knew everyone at the party within an hour.
Our daughter's a social butterfly; her teacher says she talks to everyone.

core.definition: An outgoing, friendly person who enjoys meeting people and mingling.

pronunciation.tip: Stress BUT in butterfly; the t is a quick flap, like a soft d: BUH-der-flahy.

nuance.connotation: Mostly positive or affectionate; occasionally hints that the person is shallow.
nuance.usage_note: Usually "a real/total social butterfly." Common for both adults and children. Saying it about yourself is a light way to say you love parties.

distinctions.note: The "life of the party" makes a gathering fun and gets attention; a "social butterfly" moves around talking to many people.
A "people person" enjoys and is good with people in general, including at work; a "social butterfly" is about mingling socially.

collocations: a bit of a social butterfly
the social butterfly of the office

examples.everyday: My grandma is a social butterfly; she's at the community center every day.
examples.professional: As a social butterfly, Dan was the natural choice to welcome new hires.
examples.analytical: Social butterflies tend to have wide but less dense networks, linking groups that would otherwise be separate.

nuance.analogy: Like a butterfly in a garden, landing briefly on one flower after another.
nuance.etymology: From the image of a butterfly flitting from flower to flower.
common_mistakes: Calling someone a "society butterfly" in normal conversation; "social butterfly" is the usual form.
Using it for a shy person who has many friends online; it suggests being outgoing in person.

senses: To manage to say something when someone else is talking a lot (usually in the negative).

etymology: Edgewise means sideways, edge first; the image is of squeezing a word into a tiny gap.

conversation.text: She talked for an hour. I couldn't get a word in edgewise.
Can I get a word in edgewise here?

core.definition: To find a chance to speak in a conversation that someone else is dominating.

pronunciation.tip: Stress EDGE: EJ-wahyz. American English says "edgewise"; British English says "edgeways."

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative: it complains, often humorously, about someone who talks too much.
nuance.usage_note: Almost always negative: "I couldn't get a word in edgewise," "Let me get a word in edgewise." "Can I get a word in edgewise?" is a playful way to interrupt.

distinctions.note: When someone "talks your ear off," you "can't get a word in edgewise."
"Interrupt" is the plain verb for cutting in; "get a word in edgewise" suggests it is hard to find any opening at all.

collocations: couldn't get a word in edgewise
can I get a word in edgewise
barely got a word in edgewise
never lets anyone get a word in edgewise

examples.everyday: At family dinners, my uncle never lets anyone get a word in edgewise.
examples.professional: In the call, the client was so upset that the account team couldn't get a word in edgewise.
examples.analytical: Studies of meetings show that a few people dominate the conversation, while others can't get a word in edgewise.

nuance.analogy: Like trying to slide a thin card sideways into a tight stack.
nuance.etymology: Edgewise means sideways, edge first; the image is of squeezing a word into a tiny gap.
common_mistakes: Saying "get a word in sideways" or "in edgeways" in American English; the usual US form is "edgewise".
Using it in the positive with no context ("I got a word in edgewise") sounds odd; it is mostly negative.

senses: To suddenly become very angry and lose control of your temper.

etymology: American, early 20th century; the image is of a lid or top blown off by pressure.

conversation.text: When he saw the numbers, the manager blew his top.
Don't tell Dad about the car yet. He'll blow his top.

core.definition: To explode with anger, usually loudly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TOP, with the "ah" vowel of "hot."

nuance.connotation: Negative; also slightly humorous because of the volcano image.
nuance.usage_note: Often predicted: "She's going to blow her top." Similar to "hit the roof," "fly off the handle," "blow up." It describes one outburst.

distinctions.note: "Fly off the handle" stresses how sudden the anger is; "blow one's top" stresses how explosive it is.
"Lose one's temper" is the neutral phrase; "blow one's top" is more vivid and informal.

collocations: is going to blow his top

examples.everyday: My mom blew her top when she saw the mess in the living room.
examples.professional: The coach blew his top at the referee and got ejected from the game.
examples.analytical: People rarely blow their tops over one event; usually stress builds until a small trigger sets it off.

nuance.analogy: Like a volcano or a boiling kettle whose lid flies off.
nuance.etymology: American, early 20th century; the image is of a lid or top blown off by pressure.
common_mistakes: Saying "blow one's head"; that sounds violent. It is "top" (or "blow one's stack").
Forgetting to match the possessive: "She blew her top," not "She blew his top" (unless you mean someone else).

senses: To feel extremely happy and excited (usually "be walking on air").

etymology: The image is of feeling so happy you seem weightless.

conversation.text: Since she said yes, I've been walking on air.
He got the job offer and walked on air for the rest of the week.

core.definition: To be so happy that you feel light, as if your feet aren't touching the ground.

pronunciation.tip: Stress AIR. "Walk" has a silent l: wawk.

nuance.connotation: Very positive: joy, often after good news or falling in love.
nuance.usage_note: Most common in the progressive: "I'm walking on air." Often after love, a new job, a win or a baby. Similar to "on cloud nine" and "over the moon."

distinctions.note: "On cloud nine" is a state of great happiness; "walking on air" adds a feeling of lightness and excitement. They are nearly interchangeable.
"Over the moon" is delighted about specific news; "walking on air" describes how the happiness feels.

examples.everyday: After the concert, we were walking on air all the way home.
examples.professional: The team was walking on air after landing the biggest contract in its history.
examples.analytical: The feeling of walking on air after good news is short-lived; people adapt to positive events surprisingly fast.

nuance.analogy: Like floating a few inches above the sidewalk because you feel so light.
nuance.etymology: The image is of feeling so happy you seem weightless.
common_mistakes: Saying "walking in the air"; it is "on air".
Using "on air" alone; "on air" means broadcasting on radio or TV.

word: get up on the wrong side of the bed
phonetic: /ˌɡɛt ˌʌp ɑn ðə ˌɹɔŋ ˌsaɪd əv ðə ˈbɛd/

senses: To be in a bad mood all day for no clear reason.

etymology: Said to come from an old superstition that getting out of bed on the left side brought bad luck; the details are uncertain.

conversation.text: Whoa, what's with you today? Did you get up on the wrong side of the bed?
Sorry I'm grumpy. I think I woke up on the wrong side of the bed.

core.definition: To start the day irritable and stay grumpy, without an obvious cause.

pronunciation.ipa: /ˌɡɛt ˌʌp ɑn ðə ˌɹɔŋ ˌsaɪd əv ðə ˈbɛd/
pronunciation.respelling: get uhp ahn thuh rawng sahyd uhv thuh BED
pronunciation.tip: Stress BED. "Side of the" runs together: SAHY-duhv-thuh.

nuance.connotation: Light and teasing; used about small, temporary bad moods.
nuance.usage_note: Usually past tense: "Someone got up on the wrong side of the bed." "Woke up on the wrong side of the bed" is the common variant in American speech. Saying it to someone can be playful or a little rude, depending on tone.
word_family: woke up on the wrong side of the bed (variant)
got up on the wrong side of the bed (past)

distinctions.note: "Out of sorts" means slightly unwell or not feeling like yourself; "wrong side of the bed" is specifically a bad mood.
"In a bad mood" is the plain phrase; the idiom adds the idea that it started in the morning for no reason.

collocations: someone got up on the wrong side of the bed
woke up on the wrong side of the bed
must have gotten up on the wrong side of the bed

examples.everyday: The cat must have gotten up on the wrong side of the bed; she's hissing at everyone.
examples.professional: The client seemed to have gotten up on the wrong side of the bed, so we kept the call short.
examples.analytical: What people describe as getting up on the wrong side of the bed often reflects poor sleep rather than chance.

nuance.analogy: Like the day going wrong from the very first step out of bed.
nuance.etymology: Said to come from an old superstition that getting out of bed on the left side brought bad luck; the details are uncertain.
common_mistakes: Saying "the bad side of the bed"; the idiom uses "wrong".
Using it for a serious depression; it is for a passing grumpy mood.

senses: A tight feeling in the throat caused by strong emotion, especially when you are about to cry.

etymology: A description of the physical feeling of holding back tears; in English since at least the 1800s.

conversation.text: When my daughter walked down the aisle, I had a lump in my throat.
His farewell speech left everyone with a lump in their throat.

core.definition: The choked-up feeling of being moved almost to tears.

pronunciation.tip: Stress THROAT. In use, "a lump in my throat": uh LUHM-pin my THROHT.

nuance.connotation: Emotional; usually tender (pride, love, sadness), not negative.
nuance.usage_note: Usually "have/get a lump in my throat" or "bring a lump to someone's throat." It suggests deep feeling held in, not open crying. Works in conversation and writing.

distinctions.note: "Choked up" describes the person ("I got choked up"); "a lump in one's throat" names the feeling.
"Cry one's eyes out" is crying a lot; "a lump in one's throat" is just before tears.

collocations: brought a lump to my throat
with a lump in her throat
got a lump in my throat

examples.everyday: Watching the old home videos gave me a lump in my throat.
examples.professional: The tribute to the retiring nurse put a lump in everyone's throat.
examples.analytical: The sensation of a lump in the throat comes from tightening throat muscles during strong emotion.

nuance.analogy: Like something stuck in your throat that won't let the words out.
nuance.etymology: A description of the physical feeling of holding back tears; in English since at least the 1800s.
common_mistakes: Saying "a stone in my throat" or "a ball in my throat"; the idiom is "lump".
Using it for a medical lump; in conversation it means emotion.

senses: To cry very hard for a long time.

etymology: A long-standing exaggeration of how hard someone cries.

conversation.text: I cried my eyes out at the end of that movie.
After the breakup, she stayed home and cried her eyes out.

core.definition: To weep intensely and at length, often from sadness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress EYES. "Eyes out" links: AHY-zout.

nuance.connotation: Emotional; can be serious or light (sad movies).
nuance.usage_note: Usually past tense: "I cried my eyes out." Common for movies, breakups, goodbyes. Can be said with humor about a sad film.

distinctions.note: "A lump in one's throat" is almost crying; "cry one's eyes out" is full, heavy crying.
"Burst into tears" is starting to cry suddenly; "cry one's eyes out" is crying a lot.

examples.everyday: I cried my eyes out when our dog died.
examples.professional: She admitted she cried her eyes out after the layoffs, then started job hunting the next morning.
examples.analytical: Contrary to the popular idea, people do not always feel better after crying their eyes out; context and support matter.

nuance.analogy: Like crying until you have nothing left to cry.
nuance.etymology: A long-standing exaggeration of how hard someone cries.
common_mistakes: Saying "cry out one's eyes"; the word order is "cry one's eyes out".
Mismatching the possessive: "She cried her eyes out."

senses: To end a romantic relationship with someone, or betray them, and cause them great sadness.
To make someone very sad (often "it breaks my heart").

etymology: The heart has long been the symbolic seat of love and grief; the phrase is very old in English.

conversation.text: He broke her heart when he moved away without saying goodbye.
It breaks my heart to see those dogs at the shelter.

core.definition: To cause someone deep sorrow, especially in love.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HEART. "Break" rhymes with "make."

nuance.connotation: Strongly emotional; the second sense expresses sympathy.
nuance.usage_note: "It breaks my heart to..." is a common way to express sadness or sympathy: "It breaks my heart to say this, but..." The romantic sense uses a person as subject: "She broke his heart."

distinctions.note: "Let someone down" is disappointing them; "break someone's heart" is much deeper pain.
"Heartbreaking" describes a sad situation; "break someone's heart" names the action.

examples.everyday: It breaks my heart that Grandma can't remember us anymore.
examples.professional: It breaks my heart to close the store, but the numbers don't work anymore.
examples.analytical: Songs about having one's heart broken are among the most common themes in popular music across cultures.

nuance.analogy: Like dropping something precious and fragile.
nuance.etymology: The heart has long been the symbolic seat of love and grief; the phrase is very old in English.
common_mistakes: Saying "break someone's heart into pieces" in normal speech; it is fine for emphasis, but the simple form is most natural.
Confusing "heartbroken" (adjective) and "broken-hearted" with the verb; "I was heartbroken," but "He broke my heart."

senses: To admit that something you said was wrong, often in a humbling way.

etymology: The image is of being forced to swallow what you said; recorded in English since the 1500s.

conversation.text: I said they'd never win the championship. Now I have to eat my words.
He'll eat his words when he sees how well this works.

core.definition: To take back a confident statement after it is proved wrong.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WORDS. "Words" has the r-colored ur vowel: wurdz.

nuance.connotation: Mildly humbling; often humorous or a friendly challenge.
nuance.usage_note: Common as "I had to eat my words" (admitting) and "You'll eat your words" (challenging). Close to "eat crow," which is more humiliating.

distinctions.note: "Eat crow" is a stronger American phrase for a humiliating admission; "eat one's words" is lighter.
"Take back" what you said is neutral and can be an apology; "eat one's words" means reality proved you wrong.

examples.everyday: I said I'd hate the movie, but I'm eating my words; it was great.
examples.professional: Analysts who doubted the launch are eating their words after the first quarter's numbers.
examples.analytical: Public figures rarely eat their words outright; they tend to reframe earlier predictions instead.

nuance.analogy: Like swallowing the very sentences you spoke too soon.
nuance.etymology: The image is of being forced to swallow what you said; recorded in English since the 1500s.
common_mistakes: Saying "eat my word"; it is plural: "words".
Confusing it with "mince words"; that is about speaking indirectly.

senses: To do something embarrassing or humbling, such as apologizing or asking for help, even though your pride makes it hard.

etymology: The image is of pride as something bitter you must swallow to get past.

conversation.text: I swallowed my pride and called him to apologize.
She finally swallowed her pride and asked her parents for a loan.

core.definition: To set your ego aside and do the humble thing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress PRIDE. "Swallow" is SWAH-loh.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral: it usually describes a mature, difficult choice.
nuance.usage_note: Often with "and": "I swallowed my pride and asked for help." Also "You need to swallow your pride." It suggests pride was blocking something sensible.

distinctions.note: "Eat humble pie" is being forced to admit you were wrong; "swallow one's pride" is choosing to act humbly.
"Eat one's words" is about something you said; "swallow one's pride" is about your ego in general.

collocations: too proud to swallow her pride

examples.everyday: I swallowed my pride and asked my younger brother how to set up the router.
examples.professional: The founder swallowed his pride and brought in an experienced CEO.
examples.analytical: Help-seeking research shows people often delay because they can't swallow their pride, even when help is cheap.

nuance.analogy: Like forcing down something bitter because you know it's good for you.
nuance.etymology: The image is of pride as something bitter you must swallow to get past.
common_mistakes: Saying "swallow my proud"; the noun is "pride".
Using it for being proud of something; it means setting pride aside.

senses: To firmly refuse to allow something, or insist on something, using your authority.

etymology: The image is of stamping or planting a foot to take a firm stand.

conversation.text: When the kids wanted a fourth puppy, I put my foot down.
She put her foot down: no phones at dinner.

core.definition: To take a firm stand and say no (or yes) in a way that ends the discussion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FOOT. "Put" and "foot" share the short vowel of "book."

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive: it shows firmness, sometimes bossiness.
nuance.usage_note: Typical with parents, partners and managers: "I had to put my foot down." Often followed by a colon-like explanation: "He put his foot down about curfew." (In British English it can also mean "accelerate"; that sense is rare in the US.)
word_family: put one's foot down (past is the same)

distinctions.vs: put one's foot in one's mouth
distinctions.note: "Put one's foot in one's mouth" means saying something embarrassing; don't confuse it with "put one's foot down."
"Draw the line" names the limit ("I draw the line at..."); "put one's foot down" is the act of enforcing it.

collocations: had to put her foot down
time to put your foot down

examples.everyday: After the third late night, my mom put her foot down about the curfew.
examples.professional: The CFO put her foot down and froze all nonessential travel.
examples.analytical: Parenting research suggests that putting one's foot down works best when rules are explained and applied consistently.

nuance.analogy: Like planting your foot firmly on the ground so no one can move you.
nuance.etymology: The image is of stamping or planting a foot to take a firm stand.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with "put one's foot in one's mouth."
Saying "put one's feet down"; the idiom uses the singular.

senses: Said when you know something but don't want to say who told you.

etymology: Very old; a related idea appears in Ecclesiastes 10:20, where "a bird of the air shall carry the voice."

conversation.text: "How did you know it was my birthday?" "A little bird told me."
A little bird told me you got engaged. Congratulations!

core.definition: A playful way to keep the source of some news secret.

pronunciation.tip: Stress BIRD. "Little" is LIT-l with a flapped t: LID-l.

nuance.connotation: Playful and teasing; usually about good news or gossip.
nuance.usage_note: Used as a full sentence, often with a smile. It works best for light, happy news. For sensitive information it can sound like gossip.

distinctions.note: "Hear it through the grapevine" says you heard it unofficially, through people; "a little bird told me" playfully hides who told you.
"Word of mouth" is how news spreads from person to person; "a little bird told me" is something you say.

collocations: a little bird told me that

examples.everyday: A little bird told me you're the new team captain.
examples.professional: A little bird told me the budget got approved, but let's wait for the official email.
examples.analytical: Phrases like "a little bird told me" let speakers share information while protecting their sources.

nuance.analogy: Like a bird flying by and whispering the news in your ear.
nuance.etymology: Very old; a related idea appears in Ecclesiastes 10:20, where "a bird of the air shall carry the voice."
common_mistakes: Saying "a small bird told me"; it is "little" (or "little birdie").
Using it in serious or formal reporting; it is playful.

senses: Used to promise or ask that something be kept secret.

etymology: Mum here is an old word imitating a closed-lipped sound, meaning silent; the phrase dates to at least the 1700s and is unrelated to "mum" meaning mother.

conversation.text: We're throwing her a surprise party, so mum's the word.
"Don't tell anyone." "Mum's the word."

core.definition: Keep quiet about this; I won't tell anyone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WORD. "Mum" rhymes with "gum"; it is not "mom."

nuance.connotation: Friendly and playful; used for small secrets and surprises.
nuance.usage_note: Said as a reply ("Mum's the word") or a request ("Remember, mum's the word"). Here "mum" means silent, not "mother." It is common in American English despite the British-looking "mum."

distinctions.note: "Keep something under wraps" is keeping a plan or project secret, often at work; "mum's the word" is the spoken promise.
"Zip it" is a blunt order to stop talking; "mum's the word" is about keeping a secret.

antonyms: let the cat out of the bag

examples.everyday: Mom doesn't know about the trip yet, so mum's the word.
examples.professional: The merger isn't public until Monday, so mum's the word outside this room.
examples.analytical: Phrases like "mum's the word" mark information as shared within a group and create a small bond of trust.

nuance.analogy: Like closing your lips with a soft "mmm" sound and keeping them shut.
nuance.etymology: Mum here is an old word imitating a closed-lipped sound, meaning silent; the phrase dates to at least the 1700s and is unrelated to "mum" meaning mother.
common_mistakes: Writing "mom's the word"; it is "mum", a word for silence.
Saying "mum is a word"; the fixed form is "mum's the word".

senses: To say honestly and directly what you think, even if others may not like it.

etymology: From mind in its old sense of opinion or intention.

conversation.text: Grandma always speaks her mind. You never have to guess what she thinks.
Feel free to speak your mind; we want honest feedback.

core.definition: To give your real opinion openly, without holding back.

pronunciation.tip: Stress MIND. "Speak" has a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Mostly positive (honest, brave); can hint at bluntness.
nuance.usage_note: Common in "She's not afraid to speak her mind" and "Feel free to speak your mind." Americans generally value it, but in some settings it implies the person can be blunt.

distinctions.vs: give someone a piece of one's mind
distinctions.note: "Give someone a piece of one's mind" is angry scolding; "speak one's mind" is simply being honest.
"Not mince words" stresses bluntness of wording; "speak one's mind" stresses honesty.

collocations: not afraid to speak her mind
feel free to speak your mind

examples.everyday: My roommate speaks her mind, which I appreciate even when it stings.
examples.professional: Good managers create teams where people can speak their minds without fear.
examples.analytical: Psychological safety, the sense that one can speak one's mind without penalty, is linked to better team learning.

nuance.analogy: Like opening the door to your thoughts and letting them walk out.
nuance.etymology: From mind in its old sense of opinion or intention.
common_mistakes: Saying "speak my opinion mind" or "say my mind"; the idiom is "speak my mind".
Using the plural for one person; groups "speak their minds".

senses: To believe what someone tells you without checking it or needing proof.

etymology: Word here means a statement or promise, as in "give someone your word."

conversation.text: I haven't seen the movie, but I'll take your word for it.
Don't take my word for it. Try it yourself.

core.definition: To accept that something is true because the person telling you says so.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WORD. "For it" is quick and reduced: fer-it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; often polite trust, or an invitation to check for yourself.
nuance.usage_note: "I'll take your word for it" is a friendly way to accept a claim (sometimes with mild doubt). "Don't take my word for it" invites someone to verify. You can name the thing: "I took her word for it that the store was closed."

distinctions.vs: give someone the benefit of the doubt
distinctions.note: "Give someone the benefit of the doubt" is assuming good intentions despite uncertainty; "take someone's word for it" is believing a statement.
"Take someone at their word" means believing them and acting on what they said, sometimes holding them to it.

collocations: I'll take your word for it
don't take my word for it
you'll have to take my word for it

examples.everyday: You say the soup is spicy? I'll take your word for it.
examples.professional: Don't take my word for it: here are the customer survey results.
examples.analytical: Science asks readers not to take anyone's word for it; claims should be checked against evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like accepting a check because you trust the person who signed it.
nuance.etymology: Word here means a statement or promise, as in "give someone your word."
common_mistakes: Saying "take your words for it"; it is singular: "word".
Leaving off "for it" when the thing is clear: "I'll take your word for it" is the natural full form.

senses: In trouble with someone, especially a spouse or partner, because you did something to annoy them.

etymology: American, early 20th century; the image is of being sent out to sleep with the dog. Popularized by Peter Pan, where Mr. Darling lives in the dog's kennel as penance.

conversation.text: I forgot our anniversary, so I'm in the doghouse this week.
Uh-oh, sounds like somebody's in the doghouse.

core.definition: Out of favor with someone close to you until you make up for what you did.

pronunciation.tip: Stress DOG: DAWG-hous. Some Americans say "dahg."

nuance.connotation: Humorous; used for minor offenses, especially in relationships.
nuance.usage_note: Usually "be in the doghouse (with someone)." Mostly about romantic partners, but also parents, bosses or fans. The trouble is temporary; you get "out of the doghouse" by apologizing.
word_family: doghouse (noun: a small shelter for a dog)

distinctions.note: "In hot water" is being in trouble, often serious or with authorities; "in the doghouse" is usually lighter and personal.
"On thin ice" means one more mistake will bring trouble; "in the doghouse" means you are already in trouble.

collocations: in the doghouse with his wife

examples.everyday: He's in the doghouse for leaving the gate open and letting the dog out.
examples.professional: After the missed deadline, our vendor is in the doghouse with procurement.
examples.analytical: Sports writers say a benched player is "in the coach's doghouse," stressing the personal nature of the punishment.

nuance.analogy: Like a dog sent out of the house to sleep in its little kennel until it behaves.
nuance.etymology: American, early 20th century; the image is of being sent out to sleep with the dog. Popularized by Peter Pan, where Mr. Darling lives in the dog's kennel as penance.
common_mistakes: Saying "in the dog house" with a space is common but "doghouse" is the standard spelling.
Using it for serious legal trouble; it is light and personal.

senses: To warn or scold someone very strongly that they must stop behaving badly.

etymology: From the British Riot Act of 1714: officials read part of it aloud to a crowd, which then had to disperse or face punishment.

conversation.text: Mom read us the riot act after we came home at two in the morning.
The coach read the team the riot act at halftime.

core.definition: To give someone a stern warning or reprimand, usually from a position of authority.

pronunciation.tip: Stress RIOT: RAHY-uht. "Read" here is present tense, reed (past: red).

nuance.connotation: Negative and stern; often used humorously after the fact.
nuance.usage_note: Usually about a parent, teacher, coach or boss: "She read them the riot act." It implies a serious warning: stop now, or there will be consequences.
word_family: read someone the riot act (past is the same spelling, said red)

distinctions.vs: give someone a piece of one's mind
distinctions.note: "Give someone a piece of one's mind" is personal anger; "read someone the riot act" is a stern warning, often from authority.
"Chew someone out" is angry scolding for a mistake; "read the riot act" focuses on warning against doing it again.

antonyms: give someone a pat on the back
collocations: had to read them the riot act

examples.everyday: The landlord read us the riot act about the noise.
examples.professional: After the security breach, the CIO read every department the riot act about passwords.
examples.analytical: Managers who read the riot act too often find that the warnings lose their force.

nuance.analogy: Like an official reading out a final warning before the crowd is dispersed.
nuance.etymology: From the British Riot Act of 1714: officials read part of it aloud to a crowd, which then had to disperse or face punishment.
common_mistakes: Saying "read someone a riot act"; it is "the riot act".
Using it for mild advice; it is a stern warning.

senses: To make peace after an argument and become friendly again.

etymology: From patch up, to mend with a patch, applied to relationships.

conversation.text: Did you and Sarah ever patch things up?
They had a big fight, but they patched things up over dinner.

core.definition: To repair a relationship after a disagreement, at least well enough to get along.

pronunciation.tip: Stress UP. "Patch" rhymes with "match."

nuance.connotation: Positive: it describes reconciliation, though sometimes incomplete.
nuance.usage_note: Common with "with": "I patched things up with my brother." Also "patch it up." A patch suggests a fix, not always a perfect one.

distinctions.note: "Bury the hatchet" is ending a long or serious conflict; "patch things up" is the everyday phrase for making up.
"Kiss and make up" is playful and often romantic; "patch things up" is neutral.

examples.everyday: My parents patched things up after a week of silence.
examples.professional: The two partners patched things up and agreed to keep working together.
examples.analytical: Studies of friendships find that patching things up after conflict can strengthen the bond if both sides feel heard.

nuance.analogy: Like sewing a patch over a tear in your favorite jeans: not new, but usable again.
nuance.etymology: From patch up, to mend with a patch, applied to relationships.
common_mistakes: Saying "patch up things"; it is fine, but "patch things up" is far more common.
Using it for fixing objects only; with "things" it almost always means a relationship.

senses: Very calm and relaxed, especially in a stressful situation.

etymology: Cucumbers feel cool to the touch; the comparison is recorded from the early 1700s.

conversation.text: Everyone was panicking, but the pilot was cool as a cucumber.
She walked into the exam cool as a cucumber.

core.definition: Completely calm and composed when others might be nervous.

pronunciation.tip: Stress CU: KYOO-kuhm-ber. Note the y sound: kyoo, not koo.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it praises calmness.
nuance.usage_note: Often without "as" at the start: "He was cool as a cucumber." The fuller "as cool as a cucumber" is also common. It is about calm under pressure, not about being fashionable.

distinctions.note: "Keep one's cool" is the action of staying calm; "cool as a cucumber" describes the person.
"Laid-back" is a relaxed personality in general; "cool as a cucumber" usually refers to a tense moment.

examples.everyday: My little brother was cool as a cucumber at his first piano recital.
examples.professional: The negotiator stayed cool as a cucumber while the other side raised their voices.
examples.analytical: Experienced surgeons often appear cool as a cucumber because practice reduces the stress response to routine emergencies.

nuance.analogy: Like a cucumber, which stays cool inside even on a hot day.
nuance.etymology: Cucumbers feel cool to the touch; the comparison is recorded from the early 1700s.
common_mistakes: Saying "calm as a cucumber"; the idiom is "cool".
Thinking it means stylish; here "cool" means calm.

senses: Someone who gets angry or complains when they lose.

etymology: American, early 20th century; sore in the American sense of upset or angry.

conversation.text: Don't be a sore loser. It's just Monopoly.
He threw his racket. What a sore loser.

core.definition: A person who reacts badly to losing instead of accepting it gracefully.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LOSER: LOO-zer, with a z sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it criticizes poor sportsmanship.
nuance.usage_note: Often "Don't be a sore loser" or "He's such a sore loser." Used for games, sports, elections and arguments. The opposite is "a good sport" or "a gracious loser."

distinctions.note: "Sour grapes" is pretending you didn't want what you failed to get; a "sore loser" openly complains or sulks.
A "bad sport" behaves badly in games in general; a "sore loser" specifically reacts badly to losing.

collocations: a bit of a sore loser

examples.everyday: My uncle is a sore loser at cards; he always says the deck was bad.
examples.professional: Don't be a sore loser about the lost bid; congratulate the winner and ask for feedback.
examples.analytical: Democracies depend on candidates who refuse to be sore losers and accept the results of elections.

nuance.analogy: Like a bruise that still hurts after the game is over.
nuance.etymology: American, early 20th century; sore in the American sense of upset or angry.
common_mistakes: Saying "bad loser" is also used, but "sore loser" is more common in the US.
Spelling it "soar loser"; it is "sore" (hurt).

senses: To raise a false alarm or ask for help when you don't need it, so that people stop believing you.

etymology: From Aesop's fable of the shepherd boy who falsely cried "Wolf!"; the idiom has been in English for centuries.

conversation.text: If you keep saying you're sick to skip class, nobody will believe you. Don't cry wolf.
He's cried wolf so many times that no one takes his complaints seriously.

core.definition: To keep warning of danger that isn't real, until people ignore you even when it is.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WOLF. "Wolf" has the short vowel of "wool": woolf.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it warns of losing credibility.
nuance.usage_note: Often "cry wolf too many times" or "the boy who cried wolf" (the story). Used for false alarms in families, at work and in public warnings.
word_family: the boy who cried wolf (the story)

distinctions.note: A "false alarm" is a single mistaken warning; "cry wolf" implies doing it repeatedly or on purpose.
"Sound the alarm" is warning people of a real danger; "cry wolf" is a false one.

examples.everyday: My car alarm cries wolf every time a truck drives by.
examples.professional: I don't want to cry wolf, but this bug could affect every customer.
examples.analytical: Alert fatigue in hospitals is a cry-wolf problem: too many false alarms make staff slower to respond to real ones.

nuance.analogy: Like the shepherd boy who shouted "Wolf!" for fun until no one came when a real wolf appeared.
nuance.etymology: From Aesop's fable of the shepherd boy who falsely cried "Wolf!"; the idiom has been in English for centuries.
common_mistakes: Saying "cry the wolf"; there is no article.
Using it for a single honest mistake; it suggests repeated false alarms.

senses: Fake tears or false sadness, shown to look sympathetic.

etymology: From an old belief that crocodiles weep while eating their victims; recorded in English since the 1500s.

conversation.text: Those are crocodile tears. He just wants the candy.
The senator shed crocodile tears over the plant closing he voted for.

core.definition: Insincere sorrow, displayed to gain sympathy or hide true feelings.

pronunciation.tip: Stress CROC: KRAHK-uh-dahyl. "Tears" rhymes with "fears."

nuance.connotation: Negative and critical: it accuses someone of faking.
nuance.usage_note: Common in "shed/cry crocodile tears" or "those are crocodile tears." Often used in news commentary and in families with dramatic children.

distinctions.note: "Lip service" is empty words of support; "crocodile tears" is fake sadness.
A "drama queen" overreacts; "crocodile tears" are fake, not just exaggerated.

examples.everyday: Spare me the crocodile tears; you never liked my car anyway.
examples.professional: The company's apology was dismissed as crocodile tears after the layoffs continued.
examples.analytical: Critics call public apologies crocodile tears when no change in behavior follows.

nuance.analogy: Like a crocodile that seems to weep while eating its prey.
nuance.etymology: From an old belief that crocodiles weep while eating their victims; recorded in English since the 1500s.
common_mistakes: Saying "alligator tears"; it is "crocodile".
Using it for real crying; it always means fake.

word: get along like a house on fire
phonetic: /ˌɡɛt əˌlɔŋ ˌlaɪk ə ˌhaʊs ɑn ˈfaɪɚ/

senses: To like each other very much and become friends quickly.

etymology: "Like a house on fire" first meant very fast, as a house fire spreads; the friendship sense grew from that.

conversation.text: Our kids met at camp and got along like a house on fire.
I was nervous, but my mom and my wife get along like a house on fire.

core.definition: To become close and friendly very fast, with easy conversation and shared interests.

pronunciation.ipa: /ˌɡɛt əˌlɔŋ ˌlaɪk ə ˌhaʊs ɑn ˈfaɪɚ/
pronunciation.respelling: get uh-lawng lahyk uh hous ahn FAHY-er
pronunciation.tip: Stress FIRE: FAHY-er, often almost one syllable.

nuance.connotation: Very positive.
nuance.usage_note: Also "hit it off like a house on fire." In the US, "get along" is the usual verb; British speakers say "get on like a house on fire." The fire image means fast and lively, not dangerous.
word_family: got along like a house on fire (past)

distinctions.note: "Hit it off" means getting along well from the first meeting; "like a house on fire" is more vivid and emphatic.
"Two peas in a pod" stresses how similar two people are; "get along like a house on fire" stresses how well they get along.

collocations: get along like a house on fire
got along like a house on fire
hit it off like a house on fire

examples.everyday: I thought my dog would hate the new kitten, but they get along like a house on fire.
examples.professional: The two co-founders got along like a house on fire from their first meeting.
examples.analytical: Rapid friendships, the kind where people get along like a house on fire, often rest on shared humor and similar backgrounds.

nuance.analogy: Like flames spreading fast through a wooden house: the friendship takes off quickly.
nuance.etymology: "Like a house on fire" first meant very fast, as a house fire spreads; the friendship sense grew from that.
common_mistakes: Saying "like a house in fire"; it is "on fire".
Thinking it means fighting; it means getting along very well.

word: wrap someone around one's little finger

senses: To be able to get someone to do whatever you want, usually because they love or admire you.

etymology: The image is of something so easy to control it could be wound around a little finger.

conversation.text: His daughter has him wrapped around her little finger.
The cat has the whole family wrapped around her little finger.

core.definition: To have complete influence over someone, often through charm.

pronunciation.respelling: rap suhm-wuhn uh-round wuhnz lit-l FING-ger
pronunciation.tip: Stress FINGER: FING-ger, with a hard g. The w in wrap is silent.

nuance.connotation: Usually affectionate and humorous; can suggest manipulation.
nuance.usage_note: Most common as "have someone wrapped around one's little finger." Often about children, grandparents, pets and partners. "Twist someone around one's little finger" is a less common variant.
word_family: wrapped around her little finger (adjective phrase)

distinctions.vs: in the palm of one's hand
distinctions.note: "Have someone in the palm of one's hand" means having control, often of an audience; "wrapped around one's little finger" is more personal and charming.
"Wear the pants" means being the one in charge in a household; "wrap someone around one's little finger" means being able to get your way through charm.

collocations: has him wrapped around her little finger
had the whole family wrapped around her little finger

examples.everyday: Grandpa is wrapped around my niece's little finger; she gets ice cream every visit.
examples.professional: The star client had the sales team wrapped around his little finger.
examples.analytical: Children quickly learn which adults they can wrap around their little fingers, a sign of early social intelligence.

nuance.analogy: Like a ring of string you can wind around your smallest finger without effort.
nuance.etymology: The image is of something so easy to control it could be wound around a little finger.
common_mistakes: Saying "wrapped around her small finger"; it is "little finger".
Putting the possessives on the wrong person: the controller owns the finger: "She has him wrapped around HER little finger."

senses: To become less shy and more confident and talkative.

etymology: The image is of a turtle or snail emerging from its shell.

conversation.text: Our son was quiet at first, but he's really come out of his shell this year.
She came out of her shell once she joined the softball team.

core.definition: To lose your shyness and start talking and joining in more.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SHELL. "Out of" links: OW-duhv.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it describes growth in confidence.
nuance.usage_note: Often in the present perfect: "He's really come out of his shell." Also "bring someone out of their shell." Common about children, students and new employees.
word_family: bring someone out of their shell (related)

distinctions.note: "Break the ice" is easing tension in a first conversation; "come out of one's shell" is a longer change in a shy person.
"Open up" can mean sharing feelings; "come out of one's shell" is about becoming more outgoing.

collocations: really come out of her shell
bring her out of her shell
starting to come out of their shell

examples.everyday: Drama club really helped my daughter come out of her shell.
examples.professional: The new analyst has come out of her shell and now leads the weekly standup.
examples.analytical: Children often come out of their shells when they find a group that shares their interests.

nuance.analogy: Like a turtle slowly putting its head out of its shell.
nuance.etymology: The image is of a turtle or snail emerging from its shell.
common_mistakes: Saying "come out from one's shell"; it is "out of".
Using it for someone outgoing who is just more talkative today; it implies growth from shyness.

senses: To touch on a sensitive subject and cause a strong emotional reaction (often anger or hurt).

etymology: The image is of touching an exposed nerve, which causes sharp pain.

conversation.text: I think my comment about his job struck a nerve.
Her video about student debt struck a nerve with young people.

core.definition: To mention something that a person, or many people, feel strongly about.

pronunciation.tip: Stress NERVE. "Strike a" links: STRAHY-kuh.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; negative when it upsets someone, positive when it resonates widely.
nuance.usage_note: "Hit a nerve" and "touch a nerve" are common variants. With "with," it often means something resonated widely: "The book struck a nerve with readers." Without it, it often means you upset someone.
word_family: hit a nerve / touch a nerve (variants)

distinctions.note: "Push someone's buttons" is deliberate provoking; "strike a nerve" is often accidental.
A "sore point" is the sensitive topic itself; "strike a nerve" is touching it.

examples.everyday: Asking about his dad clearly struck a nerve, so I changed the subject.
examples.professional: The ad struck a nerve with working parents and went viral.
examples.analytical: Topics that strike a nerve often relate to identity, fairness or security, which is why they spread quickly online.

nuance.analogy: Like a dentist touching a nerve in a tooth: a small touch, a big reaction.
nuance.etymology: The image is of touching an exposed nerve, which causes sharp pain.
common_mistakes: Saying "strike the nerve"; it is "a nerve".
Confusing it with "have the nerve" (to be bold or rude).

senses: To watch someone too closely and make them feel pressured.
To be close behind someone in a competition, threatening to catch up.

etymology: The image is of someone standing so close behind you that you can feel their breath, as in a close race; 20th century.

conversation.text: I can't work with my boss breathing down my neck.
The second-place team is breathing down our neck.

core.definition: To supervise someone too closely, or to be right behind them in a race.

pronunciation.tip: Stress NECK. "Breathe" (verb) ends in a voiced th and has a long ee; "breath" (noun) does not.

nuance.connotation: Negative in the first sense; tense in the second.
nuance.usage_note: Usually progressive: "He's always breathing down my neck." Used about bosses, parents, teachers and competitors. Many say "necks" for a group.

distinctions.note: "Micromanage" is the business word; "breathe down someone's neck" is the vivid everyday image.
"On someone's case" means criticizing or nagging; "breathe down someone's neck" means watching too closely.

collocations: with the boss breathing down his neck

examples.everyday: Mom was breathing down my neck while I did my homework.
examples.professional: With investors breathing down our necks, we have to show results this quarter.
examples.analytical: Close monitoring, or breathing down employees' necks, can lower motivation by signaling a lack of trust.

nuance.analogy: Like someone standing so close behind you that you feel their breath.
nuance.etymology: The image is of someone standing so close behind you that you can feel their breath, as in a close race; 20th century.
common_mistakes: Writing "breath down my neck"; the verb is "breathe".
Saying "breathe on my neck"; it is "down".

senses: To claim or suggest that someone said or meant something they did not.

etymology: The image is of placing words into someone else's mouth; versions appear in the Bible (2 Samuel 14:3) and in English since the 1500s.

conversation.text: Don't put words in my mouth. I never said I didn't like your mom.
The reporter kept trying to put words in her mouth.

core.definition: To misrepresent someone's views by stating them in your own exaggerated or wrong way.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WORDS here, and in use often MY: "Don't put words in MY mouth."

nuance.connotation: Negative: a complaint about being misquoted or misunderstood on purpose.
nuance.usage_note: Most common as the protest "Don't put words in my mouth." Also "You're putting words in my mouth." The plural "words" is fixed.
word_family: put words in someone's mouth (past is the same)

distinctions.vs: take the words right out of someone's mouth
distinctions.note: "Take the words right out of someone's mouth" is saying exactly what they were about to say (positive); "put words in someone's mouth" is wrongly claiming they said something.
"Twist someone's words" changes what they actually said; "put words in someone's mouth" invents what they didn't say.

collocations: don't put words in my mouth
tried to put words in his mouth

examples.everyday: I said the trip was expensive, not that I didn't want to go. Don't put words in my mouth.
examples.professional: Let's not put words in the client's mouth; we should ask them directly what they need.
examples.analytical: A straw man argument puts words in an opponent's mouth, attacking a position they never held.

nuance.analogy: Like a ventriloquist making a puppet say what the ventriloquist wants.
nuance.etymology: The image is of placing words into someone else's mouth; versions appear in the Bible (2 Samuel 14:3) and in English since the 1500s.
common_mistakes: Saying "put words into my mouth" is also fine, but "put words in my mouth" is more common in speech.
Using the singular "put a word in my mouth"; "put in a (good) word" is a different idiom.

word: take the words right out of someone's mouth
phonetic: /ˌteɪk ðə ˌwɝdz ˌɹaɪt ˌaʊt əv ˌsʌmwʌnz ˈmaʊθ/

senses: To say exactly what someone else was just about to say.

etymology: The image is of snatching words from someone's mouth before they can say them.

conversation.text: "Let's get pizza." "You took the words right out of my mouth."
You took the words right out of my mouth; that's exactly my concern.

core.definition: To say what another person was thinking before they could say it.

pronunciation.ipa: /ˌteɪk ðə ˌwɝdz ˌɹaɪt ˌaʊt əv ˌsʌmwʌnz ˈmaʊθ/
pronunciation.respelling: tayk thuh wurdz rahyt out uhv suhm-wuhnz MOUTH
pronunciation.tip: Stress MOUTH. "Right out of" links: rahy-TOW-duhv.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it shows agreement and connection.
nuance.usage_note: Almost always "You took the words right out of my mouth." Used as an enthusiastic way to agree. "Right" adds emphasis but can be dropped.
word_family: took the words right out of someone's mouth (past)

distinctions.note: "Put words in someone's mouth" is negative (misquoting); "take the words right out of someone's mouth" is positive (agreeing).
"You can say that again" agrees with what was just said; "you took the words right out of my mouth" adds that you were about to say it.

collocations: you took the words right out of my mouth
took the words out of my mouth

examples.everyday: "This movie is way too long." "You took the words right out of my mouth."
examples.professional: You took the words right out of my mouth: we need more time for testing.
examples.analytical: Moments when someone takes the words right out of your mouth reflect shared context and thinking.

nuance.analogy: Like reaching over and grabbing the sentence before it leaves your lips.
nuance.etymology: The image is of snatching words from someone's mouth before they can say them.
common_mistakes: Saying "took the words from my mouth"; the usual form is "out of my mouth".
Using it to complain about being interrupted; it is a happy expression of agreement.

senses: Messages or behavior that seem to mean opposite things, so it is hard to know what someone really thinks or wants.

etymology: From signals in the sense of communications; the phrase is late 20th century.

conversation.text: He texts me every day but never asks me out. I'm getting mixed signals.
Management is sending mixed signals about remote work.

core.definition: Contradictory signs about someone's feelings or intentions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SIG: SIG-nuhlz. "Mixed" is one syllable: mikst.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it describes confusion caused by inconsistency.
nuance.usage_note: Usually "send/give mixed signals" or "get mixed signals." Very common in dating and workplace talk. "Mixed messages" means the same.

distinctions.note: "Mixed feelings" are your own uncertain emotions; "mixed signals" are confusing signs from someone else.
When someone sends mixed signals, you may try to "read between the lines" to understand them.

examples.everyday: My cat sends mixed signals: she purrs and then bites my hand.
examples.professional: Leadership is sending mixed signals by praising innovation while cutting the research budget.
examples.analytical: Mixed signals from central banks can unsettle markets because investors can't predict policy.

nuance.analogy: Like traffic lights showing red and green at the same time.
nuance.etymology: From signals in the sense of communications; the phrase is late 20th century.
common_mistakes: Saying "mixing signals"; the fixed phrase is "mixed signals".
Using it for a bad phone connection only; in conversation it is about unclear intentions.

senses: To talk too much, especially in a boastful, rude or careless way.

etymology: American slang, 20th century; run here means keep going like a machine.

conversation.text: He was running his mouth all week, and then his team lost by thirty.
Stop running your mouth before you say something you'll regret.

core.definition: To talk carelessly or arrogantly, saying more than you should.

pronunciation.tip: Stress MOUTH. "Mouth" ends in a soft th, as in "think."

nuance.connotation: Negative: it criticizes boasting, gossip or rude talk.
nuance.usage_note: Common in sports and casual speech: "He's just running his mouth." Often implies the talk is empty or will cause trouble. Fairly casual; avoid in formal settings.

distinctions.note: "Talk someone's ear off" is talking too long, usually harmlessly; "run one's mouth" is careless or boastful talk.
A "big mouth" is a person who talks too much or can't keep secrets; "run one's mouth" is what they do.

examples.everyday: He ran his mouth about how easy the hike would be, then gave up halfway.
examples.professional: A player who runs his mouth on social media can become a distraction for the whole team.
examples.analytical: Trash talk, or running one's mouth, can unsettle opponents but also motivate them.

nuance.analogy: Like an engine left running that nobody bothers to turn off.
nuance.etymology: American slang, 20th century; run here means keep going like a machine.
common_mistakes: Saying "run my mouths"; it is singular for one person.
Using it as praise for a good speaker; it is always critical.

senses: Overwhelmed by a strong emotion, such as worry, grief, anger or joy, so that you can hardly control yourself.

etymology: From an old idea of being outside oneself (ecstasy, from Greek for standing outside); used in English since the 1400s.

conversation.text: When her son didn't come home, she was beside herself.
The kids were beside themselves with excitement on Christmas morning.

core.definition: So full of emotion that you are almost out of control.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SIDE: bih-SAHYD. Use the right reflexive: myself, herself, themselves.

nuance.connotation: Intense; usually worry or grief, sometimes joy (with "with").
nuance.usage_note: Usually "be beside oneself (with worry/grief/rage/excitement)." Without "with," it usually means extreme worry or distress. Note: "beside" (next to), not "besides" (in addition).

distinctions.note: "Out of one's mind (with worry)" is similar; it can also mean crazy, while "beside oneself" never does.
"Worried sick" is only worry; "beside oneself" can be any strong emotion.

examples.everyday: I was beside myself when I couldn't find my passport an hour before the flight.
examples.professional: The founders were beside themselves when the company passed a million users.
examples.analytical: People who are beside themselves with anxiety process information poorly, which is why crisis lines use short, simple steps.

nuance.analogy: Like your feelings pushing you outside your own body, so you're standing next to yourself.
nuance.etymology: From an old idea of being outside oneself (ecstasy, from Greek for standing outside); used in English since the 1400s.
common_mistakes: Saying "besides oneself"; it is "beside" (no s).
Forgetting the reflexive: say "She was beside herself," not "She was beside."

senses: To annoy or upset someone, usually by challenging them or changing something they care about.

etymology: From birds raising their feathers when alarmed or angry.

conversation.text: The new parking rules ruffled a few feathers in the neighborhood.
I don't want to ruffle any feathers, but I think we should vote again.

core.definition: To irritate or unsettle people, often mildly, by saying or doing something unwelcome.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FEATH: FETH-erz, with a voiced th as in "this."

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative; often used for unavoidable friction from change.
nuance.usage_note: Common forms: "ruffle a few feathers," "ruffle some feathers," "ruffle someone's feathers." Often admitted with some pride: "We ruffled a few feathers, but it worked." Milder than making someone angry.

distinctions.note: "Step on someone's toes" is intruding on their area; "ruffle someone's feathers" is upsetting them more generally.
"Rock the boat" is disturbing a stable situation; "ruffle feathers" is upsetting specific people.

collocations: didn't want to ruffle any feathers

examples.everyday: My sister's speech at the reunion ruffled a few feathers.
examples.professional: The new policy ruffled feathers in sales, so the VP met with each team to explain it.
examples.analytical: Reformers almost always ruffle feathers, because change threatens existing interests.

nuance.analogy: Like a bird whose feathers stand up when it is disturbed.
nuance.etymology: From birds raising their feathers when alarmed or angry.
common_mistakes: Saying "ruffle someone's feather"; it is plural: "feathers".
Using it for serious anger; it describes mild irritation.

senses: To make someone feel nervous, uneasy or slightly scared.

etymology: From creep, the feeling of something crawling on your skin; Charles Dickens used "the creeps" in David Copperfield (1850).

conversation.text: That old house at the end of the street gives me the creeps.
The way he stares at people gives me the creeps.

core.definition: To cause an uneasy, uncomfortable feeling of fear or disgust.

pronunciation.tip: Stress CREEPS, with a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it expresses unease, often about something hard to explain.
nuance.usage_note: Usually "X gives me the creeps." Used for people, places, dolls, sounds. The adjective "creepy" is closely related and very common.
