distinctions.note: "Give someone the willies" means the same and is slightly more playful.

distinctions.vs: scare the living daylights out of
distinctions.note: "Scare the living daylights out of" is a sudden big fright; "give someone the creeps" is a lingering uneasy feeling.

collocations: that place gives me the creeps

examples.everyday: Clowns give me the creeps, I'm sorry.
examples.professional: The unlit parking garage gives employees the creeps, so we're adding lights and cameras.
examples.analytical: Research on creepiness suggests that things give us the creeps when we can't predict another person's intentions.

nuance.analogy: Like the feeling of something crawling across your skin.
nuance.etymology: From creep, the feeling of something crawling on your skin; Charles Dickens used "the creeps" in David Copperfield (1850).
common_mistakes: Saying "gives me creeps"; you need "the".
Using it for a big shock; it is a creepy, uneasy feeling.

senses: To relax and enjoy yourself, behaving more freely than usual.

etymology: From the time when women wore their hair pinned up in public and let it down only in private; recorded from the 1800s.

conversation.text: It's the holiday party. Let your hair down and have fun!
On vacation, even my strict dad lets his hair down.

core.definition: To stop being formal or serious and have a good time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HAIR. "Let" and "one's" run together: LEH-wuhnz.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it encourages relaxation and fun.
nuance.usage_note: Common in invitations and encouragement: "Let your hair down!" It suits people who are usually serious, formal or busy. Applies to anyone, regardless of hair.
word_family: let one's hair down (past is the same)

distinctions.note: "Kick back" is relaxing quietly; "let one's hair down" is enjoying yourself freely, often at a party.
"Cut loose" is wilder and more energetic; "let one's hair down" is a bit gentler.

collocations: a chance to let our hair down

examples.everyday: After finals, the whole class went bowling and let their hair down.
examples.professional: The retreat gives the team a chance to let their hair down and get to know each other.
examples.analytical: Rituals like festivals give communities permission to let their hair down within safe limits.

nuance.analogy: Like taking out the pins at the end of a formal day and letting your hair fall loose.
nuance.etymology: From the time when women wore their hair pinned up in public and let it down only in private; recorded from the 1800s.
common_mistakes: Saying "let one's hairs down"; "hair" is uncountable here.
Thinking it is only about women; it is used for anyone.

word: from the bottom of one's heart

senses: Very sincerely; with deep and genuine feeling.

etymology: The heart as the center of feeling; the phrase is very old and appears in English since the 1500s.

conversation.text: Thank you from the bottom of my heart.
I'm sorry, from the bottom of my heart.

core.definition: With complete sincerity.

pronunciation.respelling: fruhm thuh bah-tuhm uhv wuhnz HAHRT
pronunciation.tip: Stress HEART. "Bottom" has a flapped t: BAH-duhm.

nuance.connotation: Warm and sincere; used for strong thanks, apologies and love.
nuance.usage_note: Most common with "thank you": "Thank you from the bottom of my heart." Also with apologies and wishes. It intensifies, so it suits serious moments rather than small favors.

distinctions.note: "Heartfelt" is the adjective ("heartfelt thanks"); "from the bottom of my heart" is the adverb phrase.
"Crocodile tears" are fake feeling, the opposite of something said from the bottom of your heart.

collocations: thank you from the bottom of my heart
from the bottom of our hearts
I mean that from the bottom of my heart

examples.everyday: To everyone who brought us meals after the surgery: thank you from the bottom of my heart.
examples.professional: From the bottom of our hearts, thank you to our volunteers for an amazing year.
examples.analytical: Formulas like "from the bottom of my heart" signal sincerity, which is why they appear so often in speeches of thanks.

nuance.analogy: Like drawing words from the deepest part of a well, not just the surface.
nuance.etymology: The heart as the center of feeling; the phrase is very old and appears in English since the 1500s.
common_mistakes: Saying "from the deep of my heart"; it is "bottom".
Using the singular "heart" for a group: say "from the bottom of our hearts."

word: one's heart goes out to someone

senses: Used to say you feel deep sympathy for someone who is suffering.

etymology: The heart as the seat of feeling; going out expresses sympathy reaching toward someone. In use since at least the 1800s.

conversation.text: My heart goes out to the families who lost their homes in the fire.
Our hearts go out to you and your family.

core.definition: I feel great sympathy and compassion for them.

pronunciation.respelling: wuhnz HAHRT gohz out tuh suhm-wuhn
pronunciation.tip: Stress HEART: "My HEART goes out to them."

nuance.connotation: Sympathetic and compassionate.
nuance.usage_note: Usually present tense with "my" or "our": "My heart goes out to..." Common in condolences, social media posts and public statements. It is sincere, but very common, so in personal messages add a specific line too.

distinctions.note: "Thoughts and prayers" is a public expression of sympathy that can sound formulaic; "my heart goes out to" is personal and warm.
"It breaks my heart" says the situation makes you very sad; "my heart goes out to them" focuses on sympathy for the people.

collocations: my heart goes out to everyone affected

examples.everyday: My heart goes out to my neighbor; her husband just passed away.
examples.professional: Our hearts go out to everyone affected by the storm, and our offices are collecting donations.
examples.analytical: Expressions like "my heart goes out to you" are part of a ritual vocabulary of sympathy that eases difficult conversations.

nuance.analogy: Like your heart reaching out toward someone to comfort them.
nuance.etymology: The heart as the seat of feeling; going out expresses sympathy reaching toward someone. In use since at least the 1800s.
common_mistakes: Saying "my heart goes to them"; you need "out".
Using the past tense in condolences ("my heart went out") sounds distant; use the present.

senses: The ability to talk easily, confidently and persuasively.

etymology: Gab is an old informal word for chatter; the phrase dates from the late 1600s.

conversation.text: My uncle could sell anything. He's got the gift of gab.
You should go into politics; you've got the gift of gab.

core.definition: A natural talent for fluent, charming conversation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress GAB, rhyming with "cab." "Gift of" links: GIF-tuhv.

nuance.connotation: Mostly positive; can hint that someone talks smoothly but not always sincerely.
nuance.usage_note: Usually "have/got the gift of gab." Americans say "gift of gab"; British English often says "gift of the gab." Common about salespeople, politicians and charming relatives.

distinctions.note: "Talk someone's ear off" is talking too much; "the gift of gab" is talking well.
A "silver tongue" is a persuasive, eloquent way of speaking, sometimes manipulative; "the gift of gab" is lighter and more casual.

collocations: born with the gift of gab

examples.everyday: My grandmother had the gift of gab; she made friends in every waiting room.
examples.professional: Recruiters with the gift of gab can still lose candidates if the offer isn't competitive.
examples.analytical: Charisma research suggests that the gift of gab matters less than listening when it comes to trust.

nuance.analogy: Like being handed a talent for talking at birth, the way some get a talent for music.
nuance.etymology: Gab is an old informal word for chatter; the phrase dates from the late 1600s.
common_mistakes: Saying "gift of gap"; it is "gab" (chatter).
Treating "gab" as formal; it is casual.
